orig_9709_s1_norm_normal_areas.description: Read normal parameters and turn continuous events into correctly standardised areas.

sections.title: Read variance, then standardise
sections.label: Standardise one boundary
sections.intro: Use continuous areas, conditional probability and binomial moments from the preceding chapters. In \(\mathrm N(\mu,\sigma^2)\), the second parameter is variance. Give probabilities to 4 decimal places and estimated measurements to 2 decimal places when labelled; calculator precision is also accepted. Exact boundary and integer fields remain exact. Written problems keep their own rounding instructions.

blocks.html:
Mean and variance have different roles

\[X\sim\mathrm N(\mu,\sigma^2),\qquad\sigma>0.\]

The mean locates the centre. The standard deviation controls spread; the variance is its square. Curves with smaller standard deviation are narrower and taller, but all have area one. For a common centre, a fixed central interval contains more probability under the narrower curve.

Standardise by the standard deviation

\[Z=\frac{X-\mu}{\sigma}\sim\mathrm N(0,1).\]

Subtract the mean and divide by σ, not σ². A value below the mean has a negative z-score. Standardise both ends of an interval separately and show the substitutions.

blocks.title: Standardise one boundary
blocks.prompt: A continuous variable follows \(\mathrm N(60,16)\). Give the exact z-score for the value \(66\).
blocks.hint: Take the standard deviation \(4\), then divide the difference from the mean by it.
blocks.solution:
Take the standard deviation \(4\), then divide the difference from the mean by it.

  • Answer: \(\frac{3}{2}\)

sections.title: Subtract cumulative areas at both boundaries
sections.label: Subtract two areas

blocks.html:
Use a consistent cumulative convention

Write \(\Phi(z)=\mathrm P(Z\le z)\). A left tail is \(\Phi(z)\); a right tail is \(1-\Phi(z)\). Symmetry gives \(\Phi(-z)=1-\Phi(z)\).

\[\begin{aligned}\mathrm P(a<X<b)&=\Phi\!\left(\frac{b-\mu}{\sigma}\right)\\&\quad-\Phi\!\left(\frac{a-\mu}{\sigma}\right).\end{aligned}\]

A table giving area between zero and z needs conversion to this cumulative convention. A quick sketch checks whether the probability should be above or below one half.

blocks.title: Subtract two areas
blocks.prompt: For a standard normal \(Z\), find \(\mathrm P(0<Z<1)\) to 4 decimal places.
blocks.hint: Subtract the cumulative area at zero from the cumulative area at one.
blocks.solution:
Subtract the cumulative area at zero from the cumulative area at one.

  • Answer: \(0.3413\)

sections.title: An exact point differs from a recorded value
sections.label: Read a point in a continuous model

blocks.html:
Density height is not point probability

A continuous model assigns probabilities to intervals through areas under its density curve. The total area is one. A single exact value has probability zero, so including or excluding an endpoint does not change a continuous area. A recorded value rounded to a unit represents an interval and can have positive probability.

Read rounding intervals as intervals

If a value is recorded to the nearest whole unit as r, its underlying value lies from \(r-0.5\) to \(r+0.5\), apart from endpoint conventions of zero probability. Do not confuse this with an exact reading \(X=r\).

blocks.title: Read a point in a continuous model
blocks.prompt: For a continuous normal variable \(X\), find \(\mathrm P(X=72)\).
blocks.hint: One exact point has zero width and contributes no area.
blocks.solution:
One exact point has zero width and contributes no area.

  • Answer: \(0\)

sections.title: Equal centres need not have equal central probabilities
sections.label: Compare spread at the same centre

blocks.html: The standardised limits are \(-\frac12\) and \(\frac12\). Take the area between them.

blocks.title: Compare spread at the same centre
blocks.prompt: \(Y\sim\mathrm N(50,16)\). Find \(\mathrm P(48<Y<52)\) to 4 decimal places.
blocks.hint: The standardised limits are \(-\frac12\) and \(\frac12\). Take the area between them.
blocks.solution:
The standardised limits are \(-\frac12\) and \(\frac12\). Take the area between them.

  • Answer: \(0.3829\)

blocks.html:
• The second normal parameter is variance, not standard deviation.
  • Subtract the lower cumulative probability from the upper one.
  • A right tail is not the left cumulative area.
  • An exact point and a rounded recording are different events.

examples.title: Read variance, then standardise
examples.question: \(X\sim\mathrm N(72,25)\). Give its standard deviation, the exact z-score for \(X=78\), and \(\mathrm P(X>78)\).
solution: Take the positive square root of the variance. Standardise by this standard deviation and complement the lower cumulative area.

examples.title: Subtract cumulative areas at both boundaries
examples.question: \(X\sim\mathrm N(80,36)\). Give the exact z-scores at 73 and 89, then \(\mathrm P(73<X<89)\).
solution: Standardise both boundaries, then subtract the lower cumulative probability from the upper.

examples.title: An exact point differs from a recorded value
examples.question: \(X\sim\mathrm N(80,25)\). Readings are recorded to the nearest 2 units. Give the exact underlying lower and upper boundaries for a recorded value 80, \(\mathrm P(X=80)\) for an exact reading, and the probability of recording 80.
solution: The recorded value represents half a recording unit on each side. An exact continuous point still has probability zero.

examples.title: Equal centres need not have equal central probabilities
examples.question: A and B are normal with common mean 80 and standard deviations 4 and 7. Find \(\mathrm P(\mid A-80\mid <5)\) and \(\mathrm P(\mid B-80\mid <5)\), then choose the correct comparison.
solution: Use each curve’s own standard deviation. By symmetry, subtract the left tail from the matching upper cumulative probability.
Correct conclusion: A is narrower and has the larger probability in this fixed central interval.

glossary.definition: The positive square root of variance.
A value with a stated cumulative probability.
The normal distribution with mean zero and variance one.
A half-unit adjustment when the normal curve represents integer counts.

revision.checks:
1. Identify the mean, variance and positive standard deviation.
  2. Sketch and label the requested region before choosing a tail or interval.
  3. Standardise each boundary using the standard deviation.
  4. Use a cumulative normal probability or inverse cumulative probability with the correct tail.
  5. For counts, check approximation conditions and apply continuity correction to the integer event.
  6. For a condition, restrict the numerator and denominator; retain full precision until the final answer.

orig_9709_s1_norm_inverse_normal.description: Recover cutoffs, means and standard deviations from lower-tail probabilities and independent equations.

sections.title: A cumulative probability determines a cutoff
sections.label: Find the median quantile
sections.intro: Use continuous areas, conditional probability and binomial moments from the preceding chapters. In \(\mathrm N(\mu,\sigma^2)\), the second parameter is variance. Give probabilities to 4 decimal places and estimated measurements to 2 decimal places when labelled; calculator precision is also accepted. Exact boundary and integer fields remain exact. Written problems keep their own rounding instructions.

blocks.html:
Convert every probability to a lower tail first

If \(\mathrm P(X\le c)=p\), use \(z=\Phi^{-1}(p)\), then \(c=\mu+\sigma z\). For an upper-tail probability α use \(p=1-\alpha\). A lower quantile below the median must have a negative z-score.

\[c=\mu+\sigma\Phi^{-1}(p).\]

blocks.title: Find the median quantile
blocks.prompt: Find the standard normal z-value with lower-tail probability \(0.5\).
blocks.hint: The distribution is symmetric about zero.
blocks.solution:
The distribution is symmetric about zero.

  • Answer: \(0\)

sections.title: Recover a mean from a known spread
sections.label: Recover the mean

blocks.html:
A known standard deviation leaves a linear equation for the mean

\[\mu=a-\sigma\Phi^{-1}(p).\]

Use the actual stated cumulative probability. Keep the z-score at calculator precision while recovering μ, then use the recovered parameters for any follow-on area.

blocks.title: Recover the mean
blocks.prompt: A normal variable has standard deviation \(4\). Its value \(54\) has the same cumulative probability as the standard normal value \(1.5\). Find its mean.
blocks.hint: The value is one and a half standard deviations above the mean.
blocks.solution:
The value is one and a half standard deviations above the mean.

  • Answer: \(48\)

sections.title: Recover a positive standard deviation
sections.label: Recover the positive spread

blocks.html:
A known mean determines the standard deviation

\[\sigma=\frac{a-\mu}{\Phi^{-1}(p)}.\]

The numerator and z-score must have compatible signs so σ is positive. A negative result is a reason to check the tail and sign, not to silently take an absolute value. Square σ only when the variance is required.

blocks.title: Recover the positive spread
blocks.prompt: A normal variable has mean \(50\). Its value \(56\) has the same cumulative probability as the standard normal value \(1.5\). Find its standard deviation.
blocks.hint: Six units equal one and a half standard deviations.
blocks.solution:
Six units equal one and a half standard deviations.

  • Answer: \(4\)

sections.title: Two quantiles determine two parameters
sections.label: Use two quantiles

blocks.html:
Two probability statements give two equations

\[\begin{aligned}a&=\mu+\sigma z_a,\\b&=\mu+\sigma z_b.\end{aligned}\]

Subtract to eliminate μ. The difference in physical cutoffs corresponds to the difference in z-scores. Recover σ first, then μ, and check both original probabilities. Equal tail probabilities for different cutoffs would not determine a positive spread.

Rounding is the final step

Rounding an intermediate quantile can move the final cutoff or parameter. Record the equations and retain full precision internally. Label whether your final answer is a standard deviation or a variance.

blocks.title: Use two quantiles
blocks.prompt: The values \(41\) and \(65\) correspond to z-scores \(-1.5\) and \(1.5\). Find the mean and standard deviation.
blocks.hint: The two values lie symmetrically about the mean, and their separation is three standard deviations.
blocks.solution:
The two values lie symmetrically about the mean, and their separation is three standard deviations.

  • Mean: \(53\)
  • Standard deviation: \(8\)

blocks.html:
• An upper-tail percentage must be complemented before inverse normal.
  • A lower quantile can require a negative z-score.
  • Do not replace a negative inferred standard deviation by its absolute value.
  • Use two independent equations to determine both parameters.

examples.title: A cumulative probability determines a cutoff
examples.question: \(X\sim\mathrm N(80,36)\). Find the standard-normal quantile z and cutoff c such that \(\mathrm P(X\le c)\)=0.95.
solution: The probability is already a lower cumulative probability. Use inverse normal, then undo standardisation.

examples.title: Recover a mean from a known spread
examples.question: X is normal with standard deviation 5 and \(\mathrm P(X\le 70)\)=0.1. Find the mean and \(\mathrm P(70<X<82)\).
solution: Write the lower-tail z-score equation and solve for the mean. Use the unrounded recovered mean in the new interval.

examples.title: Recover a positive standard deviation
examples.question: X is normal with mean 80, and \(\mathrm P(X>90)\)=0.05. Find the standard deviation, the variance, and \(\mathrm P(75<X<88)\).
solution: Convert the right tail to a lower tail before inverse normal. Divide the displacement by its z-score, checking the positive standard deviation. Retain the unrounded value for the variance and follow-on interval.

examples.title: Two quantiles determine two parameters
examples.question: X is normal, \(\mathrm P(X\le 60)\)=0.15 and \(\mathrm P(X\le 84)\)=0.85. Find its mean and standard deviation, then \(\mathrm P(60<X<84)\).
solution: Obtain two z-scores. Subtract the two standardisation equations, recover the positive spread, then substitute for the mean. The final interval is also the difference of the two given cumulative probabilities.

orig_9709_s1_norm_normal_models.description: Keep conditions and route weights explicit when normal areas feed further probability models.

sections.title: The larger tail is the conditioning space
sections.label: Divide by the conditioning area
sections.intro: Use continuous areas, conditional probability and binomial moments from the preceding chapters. In \(\mathrm N(\mu,\sigma^2)\), the second parameter is variance. Give probabilities to 4 decimal places and estimated measurements to 2 decimal places when labelled; calculator precision is also accepted. Exact boundary and integer fields remain exact. Written problems keep their own rounding instructions.

blocks.html:
Condition on the stated region

For a condition H, divide the probability of the intersection by \(\mathrm P(H)\). If \(b>a\), then \(X>b\) already implies \(X>a\).

\[\mathrm P(X>b\mid X>a)=\frac{\mathrm P(X>b)}{\mathrm P(X>a)}.\]

Using the unconditional right tail alone ignores the smaller conditional sample space.

blocks.title: Divide by the conditioning area
blocks.prompt: For a standard normal \(Z\), find \(\mathrm P(Z>1\mid Z>0)\) to 4 decimal places.
blocks.hint: The upper tail above one is contained in the positive half. Divide that tail by one half.
blocks.solution:
The upper tail above one is contained in the positive half. Divide that tail by one half.

  • Answer: \(0.3173\)

sections.title: A normal tail becomes a repeated-trial success
sections.label: Make a normal area into a count probability

blocks.html:
An interval probability can be a binomial success probability

First calculate q for one normal reading meeting its criterion. If n readings are independent with the same distribution, the number meeting that criterion is \(\mathrm B(n,q)\). Use the unrounded q in the second stage, not a rounded z-score or the original cutoff.

Expected frequencies are long-run quantities

For n comparable readings and a single-reading event probability q, the expected count is nq. It need not be an integer. Round it only if the question explicitly asks for a rounded count.

blocks.title: Make a normal area into a count probability
blocks.prompt: Four independent readings are normal with the same mean. Find the probability that exactly three readings exceed their mean.
blocks.hint: Each reading is above the mean with probability one half. Count the four possible positions of the reading below it.
blocks.solution:
Each reading is above the mean with probability one half. Count the four possible positions of the reading below it.

  • Answer: \(\frac{1}{4}\)

sections.title: Retain route weights for a posterior
sections.label: Keep the route in a posterior

blocks.html:
A mixture is assembled by routes

If a machine is selected before a reading, multiply each machine’s event probability by its selection probability and add. For a posterior machine probability, retain the relevant route as the numerator. A mixture of two normal distributions is not generally one normal distribution with averaged parameters.

blocks.title: Keep the route in a posterior
blocks.prompt: Machine A makes \(\frac35\) of the items. A and B pass inspection with probabilities \(0.9\) and \(0.7\) respectively. Given an item passes, find the probability A made it.
blocks.hint: The numerator is A's weighted passes. The denominator is the total passes from both machines.
blocks.solution:
The numerator is A's weighted passes. The denominator is the total passes from both machines.

  • Answer: \(\frac{27}{41}\)

sections.title: Condition on the physical rounding boundary
sections.label: Specify the actual boundary

blocks.html:
A rounded condition needs its own physical boundary

For nearest-unit recording, recorded \(X\ge k\) corresponds to the underlying value being at least \(k-0.5\). Intersect this with any requested recorded interval before conditioning. This rounding interval describes a measurement; it is distinct from approximating a discrete count by a continuous normal model.

blocks.title: Specify the actual boundary
blocks.prompt: A continuous measurement is rounded to the nearest whole unit. What is the lower boundary for a recorded value of at least \(75\)?
blocks.hint: The lowest measurement that rounds to seventy-five is half a unit below seventy-five.
blocks.solution:
The lowest measurement that rounds to seventy-five is half a unit below seventy-five.

  • Answer: \(\frac{149}{2}\)

blocks.html:
• A conditional denominator is the condition probability.
  • Use an unrounded single-reading probability in a repeated model.
  • A normal mixture does not generally reduce to averaged parameters.
  • A rounded threshold changes the boundary by half a recording unit.

examples.title: The larger tail is the conditioning space
examples.question: \(X\sim\mathrm N(80,36)\). Find \(\mathrm P(X>80)\), \(\mathrm P(X>89)\), and \(\mathrm P(X>89 \mid X>80)\).
solution: The smaller upper-tail event lies wholly inside the condition. Standardise each cutoff, then divide the intersection probability by the condition probability.
\[\begin{aligned}\mathrm P(X>b\mid X>a)&=\frac{\mathrm P(X>b)}{\mathrm P(X>a)},\\{}\mathrm P(X>b\mid X>a)&\approx0.1336.\end{aligned}\]

examples.title: A normal tail becomes a repeated-trial success
examples.question: \(X\sim\mathrm N(80,36)\). Take 3 independent readings and let K count those above 86. Find the single-reading probability q, \(\mathrm P(K=2)\) and \(\mathrm E(K)\).
solution: Compute the normal right tail first. Independence and an identical reading distribution then give a binomial count with that unrounded probability.

examples.title: Retain route weights for a posterior
examples.question: For each reading choose machine A with probability 0.6, otherwise B. A readings are \(\mathrm N(70,25)\); B readings are \(\mathrm N(80,36)\). Find the probability a reading is below 76, the probability it came from A given it is below 76, and the expected number below 76 in 120 independent repetitions of this selection process.
solution: Let H mean the reading is below the cutoff, and let \(q_A\), \(q_B\) be its probability under each machine. Weight the lower tails by their route probabilities. Keep only the A route for the posterior numerator.

examples.title: Condition on the physical rounding boundary
examples.question: \(X\sim\mathrm N(80,36)\). Record X to the nearest whole unit as R. Give the exact underlying boundary for \(R\ge76\), \(\mathrm P(R=80)\), and \(\mathrm P(R=80 \mid R\ge 76)\); then choose the correct point/recording statement.
solution: The condition starts half a unit below its smallest allowed recorded integer. The requested recording interval lies inside this condition, so divide its normal area by the corrected upper tail.
Correct conclusion: An exact X-value has probability zero, but a rounded recording represents an interval.

orig_9709_s1_norm_binomial_approximation.description: Check the approximation conditions and convert exact integer events to continuous strips.

sections.title: Check both strict expected-count conditions
sections.label: Check a strict approximation condition
sections.intro: Use continuous areas, conditional probability and binomial moments from the preceding chapters. In \(\mathrm N(\mu,\sigma^2)\), the second parameter is variance. Give probabilities to 4 decimal places and estimated measurements to 2 decimal places when labelled; calculator precision is also accepted. Exact boundary and integer fields remain exact. Written problems keep their own rounding instructions.

blocks.html:
Check both expected counts

For \(X\sim\mathrm B(n,p)\), this syllabus uses a normal approximation when n is sufficiently large that both \(np>5\) and \(n(1-p)>5\). Equality to 5 does not meet the stated strict criterion. Independence and a common p must still justify the underlying binomial model.

\[Y\sim\mathrm N\bigl(np,np(1-p)\bigr).\]

The second parameter is variance. Standardisation divides by the square root of that variance.

blocks.title: Check a strict approximation condition
blocks.prompt: For \(X\sim\mathrm B(20,\frac14)\), calculate the smaller of \(np\) and \(nq\).
blocks.hint: The expected count of successes is five and the expected count of failures is fifteen. The syllabus condition requires both to exceed five.
blocks.solution:
The expected count of successes is five and the expected count of failures is fifteen. The syllabus condition requires both to exceed five.

  • Answer: \(5\)

sections.title: Correct an inclusive upper tail
sections.label: Correct an inclusive tail

blocks.html:
An integer occupies a unit-width strip

Continuity correction replaces the mass at integer k by the area from \(k-0.5\) to \(k+0.5\). Sketch the bars or a number line first.

\[\begin{aligned}X\ge k&\longrightarrow Y>k-0.5,\\X\le k&\longrightarrow Y<k+0.5,\\X>k&\longrightarrow Y>k+0.5,\\X<k&\longrightarrow Y<k-0.5.\end{aligned}\]

blocks.title: Correct an inclusive tail
blocks.prompt: A binomial event is \(X\ge17\). Give the lower boundary for its normal approximation.
blocks.hint: Include the full strip for seventeen. Its lower edge is half a unit below seventeen.
blocks.solution:
Include the full strip for seventeen. Its lower edge is half a unit below seventeen.

  • Answer: \(\frac{33}{2}\)

sections.title: A strict interval needs two corrected ends
sections.label: Write both corrected endpoints

blocks.html:
Translate strict intervals before correcting

For integer bounds L and U, the event \(L<X<U\) contains \(L+1\) through \(U-1\). Its continuous strip starts at \(L+0.5\) and ends at \(U-0.5\). Do not move both boundaries in the same direction.

blocks.title: Write both corrected endpoints
blocks.prompt: Translate this integer event to the corresponding continuous interval: \(8<X<13\).
blocks.hint: Keep the first and last included integers. Extend the interval by half a unit at each end.
blocks.solution:
Keep the first and last included integers. Extend the interval by half a unit at each end.

  • Lower boundary: \(\frac{17}{2}\)
  • Upper boundary: \(\frac{25}{2}\)

sections.title: A point count becomes a strip
sections.label: Write both corrected endpoints

blocks.html:
The result remains an approximation

A normal answer need not equal the exact binomial probability. State the approximating distribution, corrected interval, z-scores and approximate area. Do not add a continuity correction to a quantity already modelled as a genuinely continuous normal reading.

blocks.title: Write both corrected endpoints
blocks.prompt: Translate this integer event to the corresponding continuous interval: \(X=10\).
blocks.hint: Keep the first and last included integers. Extend the interval by half a unit at each end.
blocks.solution:
Keep the first and last included integers. Extend the interval by half a unit at each end.

  • Lower boundary: \(\frac{19}{2}\)
  • Upper boundary: \(\frac{21}{2}\)

blocks.html:
• Both \(np\) and \(n(1-p)\) must exceed 5 under the stated criterion.
  • Use the standard deviation \(\sqrt{np(1-p)}\).
  • Exactly k requires a strip, not the zero-area point \(Y=k\).
  • An approximation is not an exact binomial calculation.

examples.title: Check both strict expected-count conditions
examples.question: \(X\sim\mathrm B(80,\frac{2}{5})\). Give \(np\) and \(n(1-p)\), then decide whether both strict expected-count conditions for the normal approximation are met.
solution: Calculate both expected counts and compare each with 5 using a strict inequality.
Correct conclusion: Both expected counts exceed 5, so the stated criterion is met.

examples.title: Correct an inclusive upper tail
examples.question: \(X\sim\mathrm B(120,\frac{1}{4})\). Give the exact corrected boundary for \(\mathrm P(X\ge 35)\), its z-score, and the normal approximation to that probability.
solution: Both expected counts exceed 5. Use the binomial mean and variance for the normal model, then divide corrected displacements by its standard deviation. This is an approximate area, not the exact binomial probability.

examples.title: A strict interval needs two corrected ends
examples.question: \(X\sim\mathrm B(120,\frac{1}{4})\). Give the exact lower and upper continuity-corrected boundaries for \(24<X<36\), then approximate its probability using a normal model.
solution: Both expected counts exceed 5. Use the binomial mean and variance for the normal model, then divide corrected displacements by its standard deviation. This is an approximate area, not the exact binomial probability.

examples.title: A point count becomes a strip
examples.question: \(X\sim\mathrm B(80,\frac{1}{2})\). Give the exact lower and upper continuity-corrected boundaries for \(X=40\), then approximate its probability using a normal model.
solution: Both expected counts exceed 5. Use the binomial mean and variance for the normal model, then divide corrected displacements by its standard deviation. This is an approximate area, not the exact binomial probability.

\[Y\sim\mathrm N\bigl(np,np(1-p)\bigr).\]

An integer occupies a unit-width strip

Continuity correction replaces the mass at integer k by the area from \(k-0.5\) to \(k+0.5\). Sketch the bars or a number line first.

Translate strict intervals before correcting

For integer bounds L and U, the event \(L<X<U\) contains \(L+1\) through \(U-1\). Its continuous strip starts at \(L+0.5\) and ends at \(U-0.5\). Do not move both boundaries in the same direction.

The result remains an approximation

A normal answer need not equal the exact binomial probability. State the approximating distribution, corrected interval, z-scores and approximate area. Do not add a continuity correction to a quantity already modelled as a genuinely continuous normal reading.
revision.checks:
1. Identify the mean, variance and positive standard deviation.
  2. Sketch and label the requested region before choosing a tail or interval.
  3. Standardise each boundary using the standard deviation.
  4. Use a cumulative normal probability or inverse cumulative probability with the correct tail.
  5. For counts, check approximation conditions and apply continuity correction to the integer event.
  6. For a condition, restrict the numerator and denominator; retain full precision until the final answer.
revision.examTip: Both \(np\) and \(n(1-p)\) must exceed 5 under the stated criterion.

sections.title: Infer a count model before approximating
sections.label: Recover the model first
sections.intro: Use continuous areas, conditional probability and binomial moments from the preceding chapters. In \(\mathrm N(\mu,\sigma^2)\), the second parameter is variance. Give probabilities to 4 decimal places and estimated measurements to 2 decimal places when labelled; calculator precision is also accepted. Exact boundary and integer fields remain exact. Written problems keep their own rounding instructions.

blocks.html:
Recover a binomial model before approximating it

If its mean and variance are given, recover p and integer n using the preceding chapter. Verify both expected counts exceed 5 before using a normal approximation. Apply continuity correction only to the final count event.

blocks.title: Recover the model first
blocks.prompt: A binomial variable has mean \(20\) and variance \(12\). Find the trial count.
blocks.hint: The failure probability is the ratio of variance to mean. Then use the mean to recover the integer trial count.
blocks.solution:
The failure probability is the ratio of variance to mean. Then use the mean to recover the integer trial count.

  • Answer: \(50\)

sections.title: A real quantile is not yet an integer decision
sections.label: Round in the required direction

blocks.html:
A continuous cutoff can imply an integer design decision

Find the real quantile first. If an integer cutoff must make a lower-tail probability at least the target, choose the smallest integer satisfying the original condition and check its predecessor. A displayed rounded quantile is not a substitute for this integer check.

blocks.title: Round in the required direction
blocks.prompt: A design requires an integer cutoff at least as large as the calculated normal quantile \(61.2\). Find the smallest allowed cutoff.
blocks.hint: Move to the next integer so that the cutoff satisfies the original lower bound.
blocks.solution:
Move to the next integer so that the cutoff satisfies the original lower bound.

  • Answer: \(62\)

sections.title: A normal trigger creates a two-level reward
sections.label: Connect the event to the payoff

blocks.html:
A normal event can trigger a discrete reward

First calculate the normal probability q of the triggering event. Build the finite reward table, then find its weighted expectation and variance. This uses the previous discrete-distribution chapter; it does not assume Statistics 2 formulae for arbitrary linear combinations of normal variables.

blocks.title: Connect the event to the payoff
blocks.prompt: A prize pays \(6\) pounds if a normal measurement exceeds its mean, otherwise nothing. Find the expected prize.
blocks.hint: The chance of exceeding the mean is one half. The only positive payment is six pounds.
blocks.solution:
The chance of exceeding the mean is one half. The only positive payment is six pounds.

  • Answer: \(3\)

sections.title: A parameter relationship closes the model
sections.label: Apply the parameter relation

blocks.html:
Relationships between parameters are extra equations

If \(\sigma=c\mu\) with \(\mu>0\), substitute into the standardised probability equation. Solve for μ and then obtain the positive σ. Check the original tail. Keep the original positive-parameter restriction throughout.

A normal model has an unbounded support

Even when a real measurement cannot be negative, its normal model may assign a small negative-tail probability. That is a limitation to assess in context, not a reason to set the model probability to zero. Distinguish an unrounded small probability from a displayed probability rounded to four decimals.

blocks.title: Apply the parameter relation
blocks.prompt: For \(X\sim\mathrm N(\mu,\sigma^2)\), \(\mu=5\sigma\). The value \(36\) has z-score \(1\). Find the standard deviation.
blocks.hint: One standard deviation above the mean is \(\mu+\sigma=6\sigma\). Set this equal to thirty-six.
blocks.solution:
One standard deviation above the mean is \(\mu+\sigma=6\sigma\). Set this equal to thirty-six.

  • Answer: \(6\)

blocks.html:
• Check feasibility of inferred binomial parameters before approximation.
  • Integer cutoffs require a neighbouring-integer check.
  • A two-level reward uses a discrete probability table.
  • A very small normal tail is not mathematically zero.

examples.title: Infer a count model before approximating
examples.question: A binomial X has mean 40 and variance 20. Recover its n and p, then give the exact continuity-corrected boundary and a normal approximation to \(\mathrm P(X\ge 45)\).
solution: Both expected counts exceed 5. Use the binomial mean and variance for the normal model, then divide corrected displacements by its standard deviation. This is an approximate area, not the exact binomial probability.

examples.title: A real quantile is not yet an integer decision
examples.question: \(X\sim\mathrm N(100,64)\). Find the real cutoff c with \(\mathrm P(X\le c)\)=0.8, the smallest integer k satisfying \(\mathrm P(X\le k)\)≥0.8, and the probability at that integer.
solution: Find the real quantile first and retain its precision. Check that the chosen integer succeeds and the previous one fails.

examples.title: A normal trigger creates a two-level reward
examples.question: \(X\sim\mathrm N(80,36)\). A reward is 15 credits if \(X>86\), otherwise 4 credits. Find the high-reward probability, mean reward and variance of the reward.
solution: Find the normal triggering probability, then build a two-value reward table and calculate its weighted moments.

examples.title: A parameter relationship closes the model
examples.question: X is normal with positive mean μ and standard deviation σ=\(\frac{1}{3}\)μ. Given \(\mathrm P(X>40)\)=0.1, find μ, σ and \(\mathrm P(X<0)\), then choose the correct model interpretation.
solution: Convert the upper tail to a cumulative quantile and substitute the given relation for σ. The normal model still has a negative tail; a displayed rounded zero is not a mathematical assertion of zero probability.
Correct conclusion: The normal model can assign a small negative tail even when physical values are non-negative.

glossary.definition: The positive square root of variance.
A value with a stated cumulative probability.
The normal distribution with mean zero and variance one.
A half-unit adjustment when the normal curve represents integer counts.
